title: After Abu Dhabi: How Europeans must reframe the European security debate – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Policy alert arguing the Trump administration has accepted Russia's demand to renegotiate the European security architecture within the Ukraine talks, walking into a trap where Moscow sets the agenda with proposals resembling its December 2021 drafts. Wesslau urges Europeans to table their own proposal quickly, anchored in Helsinki Final Act principles plus concrete deconfliction and risk-reduction measures.

themes.theme: US acceptance of Russia's architecture agenda

insights.claim: The Trump administration has accepted Russia's long-standing demand to renegotiate the European security architecture as part of negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: Raises the risk that a Ukraine deal includes NATO posture concessions affecting Europe.

insights.claim: Russia's December 2021 draft agreements demanded no further NATO enlargement (explicitly Ukraine), rolling back NATO posture to 1997, no US bases or military cooperation with non-NATO former Soviet states, no intermediate- or short-range missile deployments, and withdrawal of US nuclear weapons from Europe.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: These are the likely contours of Moscow's new proposal; useful benchmark to judge any deal.

insights.claim: By accepting the discussion and asking Moscow for proposals, the Americans have arguably walked into a trap: Russia gets to frame the debate and set the agenda at the cost of focusing on a Ukraine ceasefire.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: Agenda-setting advantage for Moscow lowers ceasefire odds and raises tail risk of a bad deal for Europe.
insights.quote: the Americans have walked into a trap

insights.claim: US negotiator Jared Kushner appears to see the logic of including Europeans when negotiating European security and has tried to get Putin to let Europeans into the room.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: A potential opening for European participation; watch whether Europeans get a seat.

insights.claim: Europeans should quickly table their own proposal for revising the European security order rather than wait for Moscow to set the framing, reaffirming Helsinki Final Act principles: territorial integrity, freedom to choose alliances and refraining from the threat of force.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: A European proposal would signal more agency in talks; watch EU summit outputs.

insights.claim: Proposed deconfliction measures include a military-to-military hotline, safe distances between aircraft and warships, commitments to use GPS and AIS transponders and refrain from jamming, no airspace violations, exercise observation/inspections and progress on arms control.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: GPS jamming and airspace incidents are live risks to aviation and shipping in the Baltic region; agreement would reduce them.

insights.claim: Moscow is unlikely to agree to the European proposal because it opposes the principles and sees an interest in escalation and unpredictability, but tabling it would still shape a discussion that will happen anyway.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: Don't expect deconfliction breakthroughs; hybrid incidents likely persist.
insights.quote: Will Moscow agree to these? Not likely.

themes.theme: Russia's strategic goals vs European red lines

insights.claim: Russia wants to revise the European security order to diminish America's commitment to Europe, gain greater control over Europe, and secure a veto over European security via a 'new Yalta' of spheres of influence.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: Underlines the long-term structural threat driving European rearmament.
insights.quote: Moscow wants a veto over European security.
insights.locator: Russia wants to revise the European

insights.claim: After Russia's invasion of Ukraine there is no scenario in which Europeans would accept less security than they have now; European security is defined in opposition to Russia, not with Russia as part of it.
insights.speaker: Fredrik Wesslau
insights.so_what: Sustained European defence spending regardless of a ceasefire.
insights.quote: European security is today defined in opposition to Russia—not with Russia as a part of it.
